hook.text: A company has $5 billion in obligations that appear nowhere on its balance sheet.

buildup.text: Operating leases, special-purpose entities, and guarantees can be kept off the main statements.

discovery.text: These items still represent real obligations—they just aren't visible at first glance.

twist.text: Enron hid billions in debt through off-balance-sheet entities. It fooled everyone for years.

climax.text: Post-Enron rules now force many off-balance-sheet items onto the books—but gaps remain.

punchline.text: What's not on the balance sheet can still sink the ship.

quiz.question: Why are off-balance-sheet items dangerous?
options: They hide real obligations from investors

details.summary: Off-balance-sheet items are financial obligations or assets that don't appear directly on the balance sheet—like operating leases (pre-ASC 842), special purpose entities, and contingent liabilities. This topic explains how companies use these to present a leaner balance sheet.
details.whyItMatters: Off-balance-sheet items can hide massive obligations from investors. Understanding them is essential because the real financial position may be significantly worse than what the balance sheet shows.
takeaways: Common off-balance-sheet items include operating leases, joint ventures, and unconsolidated subsidiaries
ASC 842 brought most leases onto the balance sheet, eliminating one major source of off-balance-sheet financing
Footnote disclosures are the primary place to find off-balance-sheet obligations

faq.question: What are off-balance-sheet items?
faq.answer: Off-balance-sheet items are financial obligations or assets not directly recorded on the balance sheet. Before ASC 842, operating leases were the most common example. Others include guarantees, unconsolidated entities, and certain derivative positions.

faq.question: Why do off-balance-sheet items matter for investors?
faq.answer: They can mask the true extent of a company's obligations. A company might appear to have low debt on its balance sheet while having billions in off-balance-sheet commitments. Enron and Lehman Brothers used off-balance-sheet structures to hide critical financial risks.
